translations.title: Why Have You Come Now...
translations.text:
Why have you come now,

youth,

life's brazen enchantment?

What brings you to the beach?

We older people were at peace

and you come to wound us, reviving

the most frightening impossible dreams,

you come to prod our imaginations.


Risen from the waves,

all shimmer, radiance, pure sensation

and the undulations of an animal lying in wait,

you advance toward shore

with tiny pink breasts,

with buttocks as mischievous as smiles,

O slender goddess with thick ankles,

and with that suggestion

(so very much your own)

of the belly giving way to the beginning

of the thighs: delicate beauty,

precise and indecisive,

where one might rest one's forehead and shed tears.


And we watch you come—vision

of a fabulous stretch of shore

with bulls, conch shells and dolphins,

on the soft sand between sea and sky,

still trembling with droplets,

dazzled by the sun and smiling.


You herald the kingdom of life,

the dream of another life, more intense and freer,

without desire festering like remorse

—without desire for you, sophisticated

little beast of a child, in whom meet

the starlet's straightforward beauty

and the prince's graceful shyness.


Though suddenly you furrow

the brow tormented by a thought

both touching and obtuse,

and turning to the sea your face, where

among wet blond locks shines

the melancholy expression of Antinous,

O indifferent beauty,

you walk along the beach as if unaware

that men and dogs follow you,

gods and angels,

and archangels,

thrones, abominations…
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: This Morning I Imagined My Death
translations.text:
This morning I imagined my death,

driving over a cliff or taking a bullet.

I felt sorry for myself. I cried over my corpse for a good while.

Then I talked about cows, the government,

how expensive life has become,

and I felt better, a little good.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: When You Feel Like Dying
translations.text:
When you feel like dying

hide your head under the pillow

and count four thousand sheep.


Go two days without eating

and you'll see how beautiful life is:

meat, beans, bread.


Go without a woman: you'll see.

When you feel like dying

don't make such a fuss: just die.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: Into the House of Day
translations.text:
Into the house of day come people and things,

foul-smelling weeds, sleepless horses,

airs with music, mannequins just like girls;

in come you, Tarumba, and I.

In comes dance. In comes the sun. A life insurance agent

and a Poet.

A policeman.

We're all going to sell ourselves, Tarumba.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: Then They Sent Sighs in Roses
translations.text:
Then they sent sighs in roses,

dove-kisses from balcony to balcony.

But the filthy night rummaged through pins,

sheets, prayers, crosses, love's mourning.


Desire lit up sour faces in the shadows.

(How many children cast away on walls,

handkerchiefs, thighs, hands, for God's sake!)


A wall of water, anguish, rose.

Red smoke in my veins. A transfigured sky.

From dust to dust I am.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: Old Is the Night
translations.text:
Old is the night, old,

long is my ancient heart.


How many arms inside

my chest, cold,

move and search for me,

my old love!


The night, old, falls

like a slow martyrdom,

shadow and star, hollow

of my chest.


And meanwhile I, absent

from my martyrdom,

go into the night, searching

for her cold body.


There has been no moon, you fools,

for centuries.

Only a brief miracle

when it is cold.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: Qasida of the Temptress
translations.text:
Everyone desires you, but no one loves you.

No one can love you, serpent,

because you have no love,

because you are dry as dry straw

and bear no fruit.

Your soul is like the skin of the old.

Resign yourself. You can do no more

than set men's hands alight

and seduce them with the promises of your body.

Rejoice. In that profession of desire

nobody can feign innocence as you do

or cast spells with your immense eyes.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: You Undress Just As
translations.text:
You undress just as if you were alone

and suddenly discover you're with me.

How I love you then

among the sheets and the cold!


You start flirting with me as with a stranger

and I court you formally and halfheartedly.

I think I'm your husband

and you're cheating on me with me.


And how we love each other then, laughing

to find ourselves alone in forbidden love!


(Afterward, when it's over, I'm afraid of you

and shiver.)
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: You Undress Just as If You Were Alone...
translations.text:
You undress just as if you were alone

and suddenly discover you're with me.

How I love you then among the sheets and the cold!


You start flirting with me as with a stranger

and I court you formally and halfheartedly.

I think I'm your husband and you're cheating on me with me.


And how we love each other then, laughing

to find ourselves alone in forbidden love!


(Afterward, when it's over, I'm afraid of you

and feel a shiver.)
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: Mouth of Tears
translations.text:
Mouth of tears, your black pupils

call me,

claim me. Your lips

kiss me without you.

How could you have

the same dark gaze

with those eyes

you wear now!


You smiled. What silence,

what a want of merriment!

How I started searching for you

in your smile, head

of earth,

lips of sadness!


You don't cry, you wouldn't cry

even if you wanted to;

you have the dimmed face

of blind women.


You can laugh. I let you

laugh, though you can't.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: How Laughingly Your Eyes Meet Mine!...
translations.text:
How laughingly your eyes make contact,

light as startled doves at the water's

edge!

How quickly your eyes make contact

with my gaze!


Who are you? What does it matter!

In spite of yourself,

there is a brief word in your eyes,

enigmatic.

I don't want to know it. I like you

looking at me sideways, hidden, frightened.

Then I can think you're fleeing something:

me or yourself, nothing,

those temptations they say pursue

a married woman.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: Doña Luz XVII
translations.text:
You will rain in the rainy season,

you will bring heat in summer,

you will bring cold at dusk.

You will die again a thousand times.


You will bloom when everything blooms.

You are nothing, no one, Mother.


The same trace will remain of us,

the seed of the wind in water,

the skeleton of leaves in the earth.

On the rocks, the tattoo of shadows,

in the heart of the trees the word love.


We are nothing, no one, Mother.

It is useless to live,

but it is more useless to die.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: Tarumba
translations.text:
I go with the ants

between the legs of flies.

I go with the ground, on the wind,

in men's shoes,

in hooves, leaves, papers;

I go where you go, Tarumba,

I come from where you come.

I know the spider.

I know what you know about yourself

and what your father knew.

I know what you've told me about myself.

I'm afraid of not knowing,

of being here like my grandmother,

staring at the wall, good and dead.

I want to go piss by moonlight.

Tarumba, it looks like rain.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: I Try to Write Your Name in the Dark...
translations.text:
I try to write your name in the dark.

I try to write that I love you.

I try to say all this in darkness.

I don't want anyone to find out,

anyone to see me at three in the morning

pacing from one side of the room to the other,

mad, full of you, in love.

Illuminated, blind, full of you, spilling you.

I say your name with all the silence of the night,

my gagged heart shouts it.

I repeat your name, say it over again,

say it tirelessly,

and I am sure that morning will come.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: Rubén Says
translations.text:
Rubén says he wants eternity, that he's fighting for a place in human memory for a century, or two, or twenty. And I think that eternity is merely a meager, impoverished prolonging of our existence.


You have to stand before a wall. And you have to know that between our pounding fists and the place they strike, there is eternity.


Believing the soul survives, or believing in human memory, is the same as believing in God, the same as carrying your plank long before the shipwreck.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: I Don't Know for Sure
translations.text:
I don't know for sure, but I suppose

that a woman and a man

someday love each other,

grow lonely little by little,

something in their hearts tells them they are alone,

alone on earth they enter each other,

they slowly kill each other.


Everything happens in silence. As

light happens inside the eye.

Love brings bodies together.

In silence they fill each other little by little.


One day they awaken, lying on arms;

then they think they know everything.

They see each other naked and they know everything.


(I don't know for sure. I suppose.)
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: It Is the Shadow of the Water
translations.text:
It is the shadow of the water

and the echo of a sigh,

trace of a glance,

memory of an absence,

a woman's nude behind glass.


She is shut in, dead—finger

of the heart, she is your ring—

far from mystery,

as easy as a child.


Drops of light filled

empty eyes,

and a body of leaves and wings

went off into the dew.


Take her with your eyes,

fill her now, my love.

She is yours as she is no one else's,

yours like suicide.


Stones I sank in the air,

wood I drowned in the river,

see my heart floating

on her simple body.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: Coveted, Forbidden
translations.text:
Coveted, forbidden,

you are near, one step away, enchantress.

With your eyes you offer yourself to whoever passes,

whoever looks at you, ripe, overflowing,

whoever asks for your body as for a grave.

Wicked young girl, virgin,

burning, closed,

I see you and love you,

your blood in tumult,

your head turning and rising,

your body horizontal on the grapes and smoke.

You are perfect, desired.

I love you and your mother when you are together.

She is still beautiful and has

what you know nothing of.

I don't know which of you I prefer

when she straightens your dress

and lets you go to look for love.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: The Little Lame Girl Is Pregnant
translations.text:
The little lame girl is pregnant.

She moves with difficulty,

but how sweet the look

with which she faces you.


Her eyes grew wider

as though her child

were growing in them too,

small and clean.

Sometimes she stops to look

at who knows what,

and her white eyes

turn pink.


She walks among all the people

with difficulty.

She cannot hide it,

but on the verge of tears,

the little lame girl suddenly

looks at her belly

and laughs. And the people laugh.


The pregnant little lame girl

is on her balcony right now

and I think she cheers herself

by singing herself a song:

“little lame girl in the right foot

and in the heart as well.”
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: That's How It Is
translations.text:
With centuries of stupor,

with centuries of hatred and tears,

with a multitude of loving, blind men,

destined for death,

drowning in my own blood, here, facedown.

Like a wounded dog surrounded by people.

Ugly as the newborn

and sad as the corpse of the woman who gave birth.


Those of us who are truly cold,

who are alone everywhere,

who have nobody,

who cannot let themselves be destroyed,

those people don't matter, are worth nothing, nothing,

let them clear out once and for all, let them die soon.

Let's see if it's true: die.

Die, Jaime, die!


Ah, you mule of a life,

stubborn, deaf!
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: You Hold Me in Your Hands
translations.text:
You hold me in your hands

and read me like a book.

You know what I don't

and tell me the things I don't tell myself.

I learn more of myself in you than in myself.

You are like a miracle at every hour,

like a pain with no place.

If you weren't a woman you'd be my friend.

Sometimes I want to tell you about women

I pursue off to one side of you.

You are like forgiveness

and I am like your son.

How kind your eyes are when you're with me!

How distant and absent you become

when I sacrifice you to solitude!

Sweet as your name, as a fig,

you wait for me in your love until I arrive.

You are like my house,

you are like my death, my love.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: What the Fuck Can I Do with My Knee?...
translations.text:
What the fuck can I do with my knee,

with my long skinny leg,

with my arms, with my tongue,

with my skinny eyes?

What can I do in this whirlpool

of well-meaning imbeciles?

What can I do with rotten clever people

and with sweet girls who want poetry instead of a man?

What can I do among poets dressed in the uniforms

of the academy or of communism?

What, among salesmen or politicians

or shepherds of souls?

What the fuck can I do, Tarumba,

if I'm neither saint nor hero nor bandit,

nor worshipper of art,

nor pharmacist,

nor rebel?

What can I do if I can do anything

and all I feel like doing is looking and looking?
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: When I Was at Sea
translations.text:
When I was at sea, of the sea was

this unhurried pain.

Give me your mouth now:

I want to eat it with your smile.


When I was in heaven, heavenly was

this urgent pain.

Give me your soul now:

I want to sink my teeth into it.


Give me nothing, love, give me nothing:

I take you in the wind,

I take you from the stream of shadow,

from the turning of light and silence,


from the skin of things

and the blood with which I climb into time.

You are a fountain whether you want to be or not

and I am the thirsty one.


Don't talk to me, if you like, don't touch me,

don't know me anymore, I no longer exist.

I am only the life that hounds you

and you are the death I resist.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: After All
translations.text:
After all—but after all—

it's only a matter of lying down together,

a matter of flesh,

of naked bodies,

the lamp of death in the world.


Glory with its throat slit, survivor

of deaf-mute time,

paltry pay for those who die together.


To the misery of pleasure, eternity,

you condemned the search, to unjust

failure you chained thirst,

you nailed the heart to a wall.


It is a matter of my body, which I bless,

against which I fight,

which must give me everything

in a stout silence

and which often dies and kills.


Solitude, mark me with your bare foot,

press my heart like grapes

and fill my mouth with its ripe liquor.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: Little One of Love
translations.text:
Little one of love, you don't know it,

you can't know it yet,

your voice does not move me,

nor the angel of your cold mouth,

nor your sandalwood reactions

in which you give out fragrance and expire,

nor your look of a virgin

crucified and burning.


Your anguish doesn't move me,

so well expressed,

nor your silent sobbing

with no way out.


Your gestures of melancholy

don't move me,

nor your longing, nor your waiting,

nor the wound

you tell me of in distress.


All of you moves me,

acting out your life

with that passion so clumsy

and so clean,

like someone who wants to kill himself

so he can say: I killed myself.


A leaf that scarcely stirs

already feels itself letting go:

I will go on loving you

all day.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: My Love, My Love, Love Found
translations.text:
My love, my love, love found

suddenly in the oyster of death.

I want to eat with you, be with you, love with you,

I want to touch you, see you.


I tell myself so, and in my body so do

the threads of my accustomed blood,

and this pain and my shoes

and my mouth and my pillow.


I love you, love, love absurdly,

foolishly, lost, radiant,

dreaming roses and inventing stars

and saying goodbye while walking beside you.


I love you from the post on the corner,

from the carpet of that empty room,

in the warm sheets of your body

where a water of poppies sleeps.


Hair of the sleepless air,

river at night, dark banana grove,

blind hive, unearthed love,


I will follow your footsteps upward,

from your feet to your thigh and side.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: The Useless Days
translations.text:
The useless days are like a crust

of grime on the soul.

There is a slow suffocation that smiles,

that forgets, that keeps quiet.

Who puts these toads on my chest

when I say nothing?

There's an idiot like me walking around,

chatting with people and ghosts,

lying down in the mud and rooting through

the shit of fame.

A snouted pig reciting verses

at family parties, where wise women

talk of love and war,

settle the question of hope.

A pig of the easy world

where deceit wants to pretend it deceives,

while slow acids

bring disgust up to the throat.

There is a man who falls for days and days,

upright, from his face,

and feels deaths and souls

growing in his chest.

A man like me who feels ashamed,

who grows tired,

who doesn't ask because he doesn't ask

or want anything.

What is all this failed tenderness doing here?

Tell it to go away!
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: The Pedestrian
translations.text:
People say, rumor has it, in drawing rooms, at parties, some person or persons in the know insist that Jaime Sabines is a great poet. Or at least a good poet. Or a decent, worthy poet. Or simply, but truly, a poet.


Jaime gets the news and is delighted: how wonderful! I'm a poet! I'm an important poet! I'm a great poet!


Convinced, he goes out into the street, or arrives home, convinced. But in the street nobody, and at home even less: nobody notices he's a poet. Why don't poets have a star on their foreheads, or a visible glow, or a ray coming out of their ears?


My God! Jaime says. I have to be a dad or a husband, or work in the factory like anyone else, or walk around like anyone else, a pedestrian.


That's it! Jaime says. I'm not a poet: I'm a pedestrian.


And this time he stays lying in bed with a sweet, quiet joy.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: It Is Nothing of Your Body
translations.text:
It is nothing of your body,

neither your skin, nor your eyes, nor your belly,

nor that secret place we both know,

grave of our death, end of our burial.

It is not your mouth—your mouth

which is just like your sex—

nor the precise meeting of your breasts,

nor your sweetest, softest back,

nor your navel where I drink.

Nor is it your thighs hard as day,

nor your ivory knees by the fire,

nor your tiny bleeding feet,

nor your scent, nor your hair.

It isn't your gaze—what is a gaze?—

sad errant light, peace without an owner,

nor the album of your ear, nor your voices,

nor the dark circles sleep leaves you.

Nor is it your viper's tongue,

an arrow of wasps in the blind air,

nor the hot dampness of your suffocation

that sustains your kiss.

It is nothing of your body,

not a blade, not a petal,

not a drop, not a grain, not a moment.


It is only this place where you were,

these stubborn arms of mine.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: Let Us Sing to Money
translations.text:
in the spirit of Christian Christmas.

Nothing is cleaner than money,

or more generous, or stronger.

Money opens every door;

it is the key to a merry life,

the rod of miracles,

the instrument of resurrection.

It gives you the necessary and the unnecessary,

bread and joy.

If your wife is sick you can cure her,

if she's a beast you can pay to have her killed.

Money washes your hands

of injustice and crime,

keeps you from work, absolves you of living.

With money in your pocket you can be yourself,

money is freedom.

If you want one woman and another and another, buy them,

if you want an island, buy it,

if you want a crowd, buy it.

(It is the cleanest verb in the language: to buy.)

I have money means I have myself.

I am mine and I am yours

in this marvelous world without resistance.

Giving money is giving love.


Hallelujah, believers, join in worship of the slandered calf

of gold, and may its mother's beautiful udders suckle us!
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: I Love You Because You Have
translations.text:
I love you because you have

the parts of a woman in just the right places

and you are complete.

You lack neither petal,

nor scent, nor shadow.

Settled in your soul,

ready to be dew on the grass of the world,

moon milk on the dark leaves.

Perhaps you see me,

maybe, one day,

in a lamp turned off,

in a corner of the room where you sleep;

I am the stain, a dot on the wall,

some line that your eyes, without you,

go on looking at.

Perhaps you recognize me

as an ancient hour

when alone you ask, you question yourself

with your body shut and without an answer.

I am a scar that no longer exists,

a kiss already washed away by time,

one love and another you have already buried.

But you are in my hands and you hold me,

and in your hands I am ember, ash,

to dry the tears of yours that I cry.

In what place, where, at what untimely hour

will you tell me that I love you? It's urgent

because our eternity is running out.

Pick up my head. Keep the arm

with which I loved your waist. Don't leave me

amid your blood on that towel.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: My Heart Sets Out
translations.text:
My heart sets out from my body to yours

on its last journey.

Offshoot of light,

water of the ages that is born lost in you.

Come to my thirst. Now.

After everything. Before.

Come to my long thirst held at bay

by mouths, scant springs.

I want that deep harp that in your belly

lulls wild children,

I want that taut wetness throbbing in you,

that wetness of water that burns in you.

Woman, soft muscle.

The skin of a kiss between your breasts

with their darkened swell

sails in my mouth

and measures blood.

You too. And it's not too late.

We can still die in each other:

that place belonging to no one is yours and mine.

Woman, tenderness of hatred, ancient mother,

I want to enter, penetrate you,

poison, flame, absence,

bitter and bitter sea, pass through you.

Each cell is female, open earth,

open water, something opening.

I was born to enter you.

I am the arrow in the back of the dying gazelle.

I exist to know you,

a grain of anguish in a bird's heart.

I will be over you, and all women

will have a man over them everywhere.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: I Love You at Ten in the Morning
translations.text:
I love you at ten in the morning, and at eleven, and at noon. I love you with all my soul and all my body, sometimes, on rainy afternoons. But at two in the afternoon, or at three, when I start thinking about the two of us, and you are thinking about food or daily work or the amusements you don't have, I begin to hate you inwardly, with half the hatred I keep for myself.


Then I love you again, when we lie down and I feel you were made for me, that somehow your knee and belly tell me so, that my hands convince me of it, and that there's no better place for me to come, for me to go, than your body. You come to meet me with your whole self, and we both disappear for an instant, go into the mouth of God, until I tell you I'm hungry or sleepy.


Every day I love you and hate you beyond remedy. And there are days too, hours, when I don't know you, when you're as strange to me as another man's wife. I worry about men, I worry about myself, my sorrows distract me. I may not think of you for a long time. You see. Who could love you less than I do, my love?
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: Miss X
translations.text:
Miss X, yes, the little Miss X,

came at last to my hope:

around her eyes,

brief, infinite, knowing nothing.

She is nimble and clean as the gentle

wind at dawn,

cheerful and soft and deep

like grass under water.

She grows sad sometimes

with that mural sadness that on her face

makes quick idols

and draws troubled ghosts.

I think she is like a little girl

asking an old woman questions,

like a scatterbrained little donkey

entering a city, full of straw.

She also has a grown woman

who suddenly frightens her gaze

and stirs inside her and undoes

her insides with bites of weeping.

Miss X, yes, the one who laughs with me

and won't tell me her name,

has now told me, standing on her shadow,

that she loves me but doesn't love me.

I let her shake her head,

saying no and no, since she tires me that way,

and my kiss on her hand sprouts

peacefully beneath the skin, a seed of wings.

Yesterday the light was

wet all day,

and Miss X went out with a cape

over her shoulders, light, in love.

She has never been such a child, never

a lover so loved in all time.

Her hair fell over her forehead,

over her eyes, my soul.


I took her hand, and we walked

all the afternoon of water.


Ah, Miss X, Miss X, hidden

flower of dawn!


You will not love her, sir, you don't know how.

I will see her tomorrow.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: Daimon Atopon
translations.text:
For Marifé and Pepe Piera
I
One may
		search for you beneath a cypress of foam,
in the fingers of the air,
		the metallic air of dream,
in a volcano of birds set ablaze with snow
or
		in the voiceless waves of silver fish.


You hide in rivers,
in leaves of stone,
in frozen
		moons.
You live behind the veins,
at the edge of the teeth,

		invisible in the naked blood of dawn.


I have often seen you burn in windowpanes,
leap in the
		pupils,
burn away in the echoes of an unnamable abyss.


Your shadow gave me light,
caressed my forehead,
took on a body in my
		mouth.
And your gaze burns, lightning of ice,
smoke in the eyebrows,

		lava.
II

		Tree of forgetting, you,
unceasing body,
dove suspended above the
		vertigo.
There is a blue salt behind your eyebrows,
a sea of open
		fire in your cheeks,
and an unspeakable ticking that takes me
to a
		deep god made of foam.


And it is to scan the air,
scratch at mystery,
stab the shadow.


And I slowly discover you,
metallic woman, among the hawthorn:
a
		murmur of transparent blood
in the lost face of silence.
III
Through
		you light rises at midday,

sand stretching to my lips,
a thread of burning
		hurrying earth

where space wells up more intensely.
It is a geyser of foam,

		of interrupted lava,
of an incomplete dove
that multiplies the air
		into a dimension of voices.


Everything is music, note, tuning fork.
Even bodies, in nothingness,
		resound.


From “Canon,” 1973

translations.title: Acis and Galatea
translations.text:
Daimon Atopon

		For Marifé and Pepe Piera
I
One may
		search for you beneath a cypress of foam,
in the fingers of the air,
		the metallic air of dream,
in a volcano of birds set ablaze with snow
or
		in the voiceless waves of silver fish.


You hide in rivers,
in leaves of stone,
in frozen
		moons.
You live behind the veins,
at the edge of the teeth,

		invisible in the naked blood of dawn.


I have often seen you burn in windowpanes,
leap in the
		pupils,
burn away in the echoes of an unnamable abyss.


Your shadow gave me light,
caressed my forehead,
took on a body in my
		mouth.
And your gaze burns, lightning of ice,
smoke in the eyebrows,

		lava.

translations.title: Love
translations.text:
To escape you
there are
		no longer steps enough,
tunnels, planes,
telephones or ships.
Everything
		that goes away
with a man who escapes:
silence, the voice,
the
		trains and the years,
cannot help me flee
this precise enclosure

		—without hours or a clock,
without windows or pictures—
which everywhere
		goes
with me when I travel.


To escape you
I need a weariness
born of you yourself:

		a doubt, a grudge,
the shame of weeping;
the fear I
		felt
—for instance—when I set
upon your fragile name
the
		wrong, hard,
abrupt shape of my lips…

translations.title: Continuing Life
translations.text:
Tree that you are, a painful flash of lightning,
wind that snatches up burning
		matter,
forests of lightning in the night water:
must I tell you
		that there is being forged for me
a heavy jewel in my heart, a blade

		that cleaves the shelter of the blood like a star?


I know no other gaze than one like a flight,
restful and deep,
		I know no other distant footstep,
no wave clearer than the life in my
		chest.


Know I am living, clouds, know that I sing,
beneath the
		confused glory of the afternoon, alone.


Know I am living, that the sky presses on me,
that my forehead
		must fall like an empty lamp
at the feet of a statue that keeps
		tenacious watch.
From
		“” 1989

translations.title: Epitaph
translations.text:
Two
		profiles, there are two, in the motionless
repose of the sharp-featured gentleman,
but
		just one profile, the true one,
makes up the coin of his death.


Coin of life—chance and fortune—
it has played out its sad and
		austere fall,
and there lies the most sincere lover,
waiting for a love to
		wake him.


Now faithful lines and strokes sum up
his vigorous, so
		delicate dying,
a lover consumed in forgettings.


What fragrance of kisses he has never given.
Oh, brave and singular
		perfume.
Oh, to die with the scent of one in love.
